sources.news_title: Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown
New Epstein files bill reached number of signatures needed to force House vote, says congressman
sources.text:
Rabia Iclal Turan
11 November 2026•Update: 11 November 2026
US Republican Representative Thomas Massie said Wednesday that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II has reached 218 signatures, the threshold needed to force a vote in the House of Representatives.
“This morning we reached the required 218 signatures on my discharge petition for Epstein Files Transparency Act II!” Massie said on US social media platform X.
The Kentucky Republican said he is working with Democratic Representatives Pramila Jayapal, Teresa Leger Fernandez, and Ro Khanna to “get this to the floor for a vote soon.” he said.
Massie introduced the bill on July 15 with Khanna and Leger Fernandez. Democratic Senators Jeff Merkley and Ben Ray Lujan are leading the Senate version.
The bill would let state attorneys general, district attorneys, members of Congress, and Epstein’s victims sue the US attorney general for withholding, redacting, delaying, or failing to publish Epstein-related records.
It would also give victims access to full, unredacted records about themselves, including FBI interview reports. It would require the Justice Department to give state and local prosecutors the unredacted records they need, including secure access to classified materials.
“Since the Epstein Files Transparency Act was signed into law on November 19, 2025, the Department of Justice has flagrantly and consistently ignored EFTA’s disclosure requirements,” Massie said in a July 15 statement introducing the bill.
“The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public. In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing,” he added.

sources.news_title: Massie Successfully Forces Another Epstein Files Vote
sources.text:
Rep. Thomas Massie has successfully forced a second House vote to facilitate the release of files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.
The measure, dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, will come up for a vote in the coming weeks after Massie circulated another discharge petition, a process that places a piece of legislation in front of the full House if more than half of all House members sign it.
The legislation gives state attorneys general the power to represent victims of Epstein’s abuse and sue the Justice Department for failing to comply with a previous law — also championed by Massie — that compelled the department to release all of its Epstein-related documents.
Rep. John Garamendi (D-California) was the last Democratic signature Wednesday, one day after Rep. Adam Smith (D-Washington) added his name. Most Democrats, as well as four Republicans, had signed the petition ahead of the weekslong congressional recess before the midterms.
Trending
Garamendi’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Massie celebrated hitting the required number of signatures on Wednesday on X, saying he was working with several other lawmakers to get the legislation “to the floor for a vote soon.”
Garamendi and Smith signed a separate discharge petition last year to help pass the original Epstein Files Transparency Act, sponsored by Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California).

sources.news_title: Massie announces he has enough signatures for discharge petition for Epstein Files part 2
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Kentucky GOP Rep. Thomas Massie announced Wednesday that he got enough signatures for his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II.
He said he was working with Democratic Reps. Ro Khanna (California), Teresa Leger Fernandez (New Mexico) and Pramila Jayapal (Washington) to get the discharge petition to the floor for a vote.
Massie said that with the discharge petition he is filing, it will allow survivors of disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein to get access to their own records.
Last year Massie and Khanna were behind the effort to release the files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, resulting in President Donald Trump signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act.
Epstein was convicted of sex trafficking in 2019, the same year he died in prison.
In accordance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, the DOJ released millions of documents on Epstein and who he was associated with. However, lawmakers have objected, stating that some names are still redacted.

sources.news_title: Massie secures signatures to force vote on second Epstein files petition
Another bill to release Epstein files headed to House floor
sources.text:
Another bill to release Epstein files headed to House floor
Discharge petition from GOP Rep. Thomas Massie has enough signatures to move to a vote
As Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.
Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.
Earlier this week, Massie said his pitch to his colleagues was simple.
“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he said, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.
Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.
The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.
The bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.
In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.
The new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.
Now that the new petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.
Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.
Allies of the issue in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”
“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it,” Massie said. “There’s nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor.”
